19669-twenty-years-of-balkan-tangle:
M. Edith Durham was a British traveler who knew the Balkans better than most outsiders. Twenty Years of Balkan Tangle grew from her journeys through the Near East. It opens with a sea trip among mauve islets in a dazzling blue sea. Strange tongues and stranger garments greeted her at each port. She writes that the fascination of the region took hold of her there.

Durham spent years among Albanians and their neighbors. She learned languages, recorded customs, and took sides in local causes. The Balkans of her years there were a knot of empires and new nations. Her book untangles that knot from ground level. It stays a key eyewitness source for the region.
19705-border-and-bastille:
Border and Bastille is a nineteenth-century memoir of travel and hardship. Its author thanks patrons who helped him reach the post he wanted. He admits one benefactor kindly overrated his qualifications. Such prefaces were the era's way of settling debts in print. The title joins a border crossing with a prison, the Bastille. Both promise trouble met on the road.

Memoirs of this kind fed a public hungry for foreign scenes. A border meant new laws, new tongues, and new risks. A prison meant the state showing its teeth. The author moves between gratitude and grievance in his opening. That mix often signals a life spent seeking favor abroad. The book belongs to the confessional travel shelf of its century.
19711-the-buried-temple:
Maurice Maeterlinck was a Belgian writer who won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The Buried Temple gathers his essays on moral and unseen forces. One passage asks whether an intelligent Judge must exist. It wonders whether cheating a neighbor cheats all the forces of justice too. Maeterlinck writes philosophy as quiet, searching prose.

His essays circle death, fate, silence, and the soul. The buried temple of the title is the hidden shrine within each person. Readers meet symbolist thought at its most gentle. Maeterlinck avoids system and proof on purpose. He prefers wonder that stays honest about mystery. The book is a calm entry into his meditative work.
19824-horses-nine-stories-of-harness-and:
Sewell Ford's Horses, from 1903, collects nine stories of harness and saddle. One hero, Skipper, joins the force at the age of six. He is clean of limb and sound of wind, without a blemish. A Green Mountain boy broke him to saddle. That boy knew more of horse nature than of trashy book learning. Ford's horses are working animals with full characters.

Ford wrote beloved animal stories set in New York and Vermont. His horses pull cabs, carry police, and haul loads. Each story tests the bond between horse and driver. The age of the horse was ending as he wrote. These tales preserve its skills and affections. Readers meet horsepower when it still had a heartbeat.
20054-the-mermaid-a-love-tale:
L. Dougall published The Mermaid, a love tale, in 1895. Its lead man, Caius Simpson, is the only son of a farmer. The farm lies on the north-west coast of Prince Edward's Island. His father worked hard, grew rich by island standards, and made his land yield well.

From that firm ground, a love story grows in a sea-bound place. Island farms, coasts, and small towns shape the lives on the page. The title hints at myth and the pull of the sea. Readers get romance rooted in work, land, and local custom.
20170-legend-land-vol-1-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume one, gathers old tales of the West of England. Years ago, a rich, lovely lady came at times to one church. No one knew where she came from or who she was. Her beauty and glorious voice set the whole parish talking of her.

Such mystery figures walk through many tales in this set. Old churches, moors, and coasts of the West Country frame them. The book saves tales told by word of mouth for print readers. Readers get ghosts, saints, and wonders from a land rich in legend.
20180-mr-kris-kringle-a-christmas-tale:
Mr. Kris Kringle is a Christmas tale named for Santa Claus himself. A touch of sadness dims the children's usual gay Christmas humor. That hopeful hour, so bright for the young, carries shadow here. Years bring such shadow to joy, the tale notes at its start.

Christmas tales of this era mix gifts with grief and grace. Poor children, kind strangers, and small miracles fill many such stories. The book aims to warm hearts while it tugs at them too. Readers get a tender holiday tale in the classic sentimental vein.
20214-instruction-for-using-a-slide-rule:
Instruction for Using a Slide Rule teaches a tool once vital to skilled work. Slide rules gave fast, close answers without long hand sums. Students, teachers, engineers, and architects all used them daily, it notes. Draftsmen, surveyors, and chemists found the rule just as handy at work.

Clerks and accountants used it when rough sums had to be rapid. The manual explains scales, settings, and worked examples step by step. Before electronic calculators, this slim tool ruled offices and labs. Readers get a clear fossil of practical math in the pre-digital age.
20249-legend-land-vol-2-being-a-collecti:
Legend Land, volume two, gathers more old tales of the West of England. Brent Tor rises as a lone, church-crowned peak near Lydford. It stands like a sentry watching the West for grim Dartmoor. From afar, the brave little hill looks like a burst of flame.

Burnt Tor, they say, was its old name for just that reason. Saints, giants, and ghosts crowd the tales tied to such places. Each short piece ties a story to a tor, church, or moor. Readers get a second rich helping of West Country legend and lore.
20255-the-unruly-sprite-a-partial-fairy-:
Henry van Dyke wrote The Unruly Sprite, a partial fairy tale of visions and faith. Some beings in the tale seem as substantial as mountain mists. They flicker and stray like will-o'-the-wisps over dark, wet ground. Yet something immortal clings to them, the man in the tale knows.

Without their presence, the world would be nothing to him at all. Van Dyke blends fairy lore with gentle moral and spiritual counsel. His sprite stands for the wild, bright part of the soul. Readers get a short, lyrical tale from a beloved American essayist-preacher.
20314-pearl-and-periwinkle:
Pearl and Periwinkle is a children's tale of two orphans taken into a stiff home. The children are son and daughter of the family's outcast sister. She has been half-forgotten, though only two months dead, the book notes. Adopting her children strikes Miss Hetty as almost scandalous at first.

Worse still, the pair have traveled all their young lives with a circus. Circus ways clash with a prim household's rules and manners at once. Yet pathos softens that clash as the tale goes on. Young readers get a story of orphans, pride, and slowly opening hearts.
20328-simon-dale:
Anthony Hope wrote Simon Dale, a historical novel of Restoration England. It opens by praising a great man who left an enduring name. His rule for life was charity in mind, trust in providence. And truth as the pole on which a life should turn, it adds.

Simon Dale serves at the court of Charles the Second in this tale. Hope, famed for The Prisoner of Zenda, loved courts and swordplay. Love, honor, and intrigue swirl around his young hero at Whitehall. Readers get polished historical romance from a master of the form.
20563-terry-a-tale-of-the-hill-people:
Charles Goff Thomson's Terry: A Tale of the Hill People opens with a shot in the winter hills. The frosty silence of the snow-covered hills is broken by the vicious crack of a high-powered, small-caliber rifle. A hidden hunter has fired from a thicket.

The hunter springs out and crosses the gully to a knoll. There lies a black furry bundle, the game he has brought down. Thomson builds his tale of the hill people on such scenes of hunting, hardship, and mountain custom. The hills themselves, white and silent, shape every life in the story.
20567-the-pigeon-tale:
Virginia Bennett's The Pigeon Tale is a story for children set in an old farmhouse that seems to wake up and dress itself young again. The fresh muslin curtains at the window are stiff with starch. They will not stir an inch in the breeze blowing in.

The old farmhouse, the narrator decides, is trying to look young again. To look young again: how many others wish the same. Into that brightened house comes the pigeon's tale, told in Bennett's gentle farm language. The book belongs to the shelf of quiet animal and farm stories written for young readers.
20580-napoleon-the-little:
Victor Hugo wrote Napoleon the Little as a furious attack on Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte after his coup of December 1851. Hugo, driven into exile, refused to call the new ruler Napoleon the Great's equal. This 1909 edition brought the polemic to English readers in a fresh form.

Its pages stage scenes from the fall of the republic. The representatives crowd the right lobby of the Assembly and return to their places, leaving the passage free. It was about four in the afternoon, and darkness was falling on the great hall. Hugo turns such scenes into an indictment of tyranny.
20709-from-pole-to-pole-a-book-for-young:
Sven Hedin, the Swedish explorer of Central Asia, wrote From Pole to Pole as a book of world travel for young people. Rather than tell his own expeditions, he takes readers on one great journey around the earth. Lands, peoples, and natural wonders pass in order along the route.

Our journey begins at Stockholm, the capital of my native country, he writes. Leaving Stockholm by train in the evening, we travel all night in comfortable sleeping cars. We arrive next morning at Trelleborg, Sweden's southernmost port, where the journey by sea begins. School readers across Europe learned geography from Hedin's ride.
20711-daily-thoughts-selected-from-the-w:
Daily Thoughts gathers short passages from the writings of Charles Kingsley, chosen for one day at a time. Kingsley was a clergyman, novelist, and naturalist whose sermons and books filled Victorian homes. A daily reading book lets his voice speak briefly each morning.

Kingsley urges readers to understand where we are, and what our work is here. He scorns superstitions about the good old times. Men fancy those days belonged to God, he says, while this age belongs only to man, blind chance, and the evil one. The selections mix devotion, nature, and social duty in his hearty style.
20716-the-tale-of-timothy-turtle:
Arthur Scott Bailey's The Tale of Timothy Turtle belongs to his Sleepy-Time Tales of the animals of Pleasant Valley. Timothy Turtle is an old, grumpy resident of Black Creek. All the wild folk know him by name, though few see much of him.

He is seen less often than Mr. Crow because he spends much of his time on the muddy bottom of Black Creek. Besides, he never flapped his way through the air to Farmer Green's fields. Bailey's animal tales taught children the habits of real creatures while dressing them in waistcoats of story.
20808-three-people:
A baby fresh from the bath, all curls and blue eyes, opens Three People. Isabella Alden, who wrote as Pansy, asks what such a child could be but a beauty. Hands, feet, and a rosebud mouth all quiver with life and glee.

Pansy wrote Christian tales for vast numbers of young readers. Three People weaves faith into home life and the growth of its leads. Her books taught conduct through story rather than sermon. This one keeps her warm tone and clear moral aim. It shows why her tales filled Sunday school shelves and family bookcases across America for decades.
20878-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-essay-:
Thomas Carlyle's works, says John Morley, form a canon closed and set for posterity. Thirty fine volumes hold his Gospel of Silence in compressed form. Morley's essay on Carlyle, in Critical Miscellanies, weighs that vast, strange legacy.

Carlyle thundered against his age as prophet, historian, and sage of Chelsea. Morley sorts his power from his faults with cool, clear judgment. Hero worship, German thought, and French revolt all fed Carlyle's fire. This essay gives new readers a firm guide into a writer who awed and irked his century in near equal parts.
20923-a-negro-explorer-at-the-north-pole:
Word that Matt Henson stood with Peary at the North Pole reached New York in 1909, this book recalls. A Peary Arctic Club man swore Henson must have been there that day. A Negro Explorer at the North Pole, from 1912, tells Henson's own tale.

Henson, a Black explorer of rare skill, drove dogs and broke trail for Peary. Cold, hunger, and ice perils fill his plain, strong account. White fame long slighted his share in the feat. His book claims that share with calm proof, and it remains a key voice from the heroic age of polar travel.
20939-the-song-of-the-exile:
England's shores shrink astern as The Song of the Exile opens in verse of parting pain. The singer owns he has little cause to mourn, for home gave him only unrest. Birth, yes, his native land gave, but never a true home.

Visions and miscellaneous poems fill the rest of this slight volume's pages. Exile, faith, loss, and hope sound through its gathered pieces in turn. Such verse spoke to many in an age of wide migration and parting. Readers meet a voice that turns private sorrow into song, plain in feeling even when its dress is old and formal.
21105-teddy-the-story-of-a-little-pickle:
John Conran Hutcheson wrote this short children's book about Teddy. The small boy's loud demand for his grandmother startles a railway porter out of his skin. Teddy is an independent young gentleman of about ten or eleven in spirit, forever in minor trouble. His small misdeeds fill most of the chapters.

The porter who first meets him is a tall, good-natured giant in worn velveteen clothes smeared with oil and grease. Hutcheson, better known for sea tales, keeps this story on land and at child height. It aims at young readers who enjoy seeing a pickle of a boy get into and out of scrapes.
21129-the-heart-of-una-sackville:
Una Sackville starts a diary in May 1895, in a handsome book with a clasp and key given her by Lena Streatham. Mrs George de Horne Vaizey tells Una's story through that diary, begun just as she leaves school. Una means to write only when she wants to talk and her friend Lorna is not near.

The tale follows a young woman of the professional middle classes. She looks for love and a husband in the months and years after school. Vaizey draws the men and women around Una sharply. Written close to its 1895 setting, it records the social world of such girls from inside.
21203-the-tale-of-grandfather-mole:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales introduce a queer old person who has lived in Farmer Green's garden longer than anyone can say. Neighbours seldom saw Grandfather Mole, since moles spend their lives underground. The frontispiece shows him making a rush at Mr. Meadow Mouse.

Bailey wrote a whole shelf of these animal tales, from Cuffy Bear to Dickie Deer Mouse, for Grosset and Dunlap. Each gives one creature a small comedy of habits, appetites, and quarrels with the neighbours. Grandfather Mole's grumbling ways underground make him a funny, cross old character for children hearing the stories at bedtime.
21272-the-bibliotaph-and-other-people:
Leon H. Vincent's essays on book lovers appeared in Boston in 1899, several of them first printed in the Atlantic Monthly. The Bibliotaph, his opening portrait, is a book collector buried in his books, drawn not wholly from imagination. Two more papers follow the same figure among his friends, scrapbooks, and bargain bins.

Other essays read the letters of John Keats and consider Thomas Hardy and an Elizabethan novelist. A third takes up Stevenson as vagabond and philosopher, ending with his novel St Ives. Vincent pokes gentle fun at collectors while sharing their passion. The volume preserves the talk of 1890s book rooms, where bargains and editions were serious sport.
21296-mother-carey-s-chicken-her-voyage-:
Mark Strong has always longed to follow his sea-captain father to sea. At last his father agrees to take both Mark and his mother on the next voyage. George Manville Fenn warns the boy that a man's duty is to face danger. A woman, he says, keeps the nest. But the family sails together anyway. The Java Seas await them.

Pirates, sharks, serpents, volcanoes, hostile peoples, geysers, and fire at sea crowd the voyage to the unknown isle of the title. Fenn piles peril on peril in his practised way. Mother Carey's chicken, a storm petrel, gives the tale its name and its sea flavour.
21314-king-o-the-beach-a-tropic-tale:
Carey, a teenage boy, sails on the steamer Chusan to join his parents in Australia in George Manville Fenn's tropic tale. He befriends the ship's doctor and seaman Bob Bostock. Then he falls from the rigging and is knocked out, his telescope taking the worst of the fall. A gale then drives the powerless ship onto a coral-girt volcanic island.

Most passengers escape by boat, but Carey is too hurt to move, so the doctor and Bostock stay with him on the wreck. A beachcomber who calls himself king of the islands arrives with a retinue and proves vicious. When he shoots the doctor, the tale turns toward rescue.
21333-doom-castle:
Neil Munro's novel of Jacobite Scotland opens on an autumn afternoon with wintry breakers sounding and nuts dropping in the corries of Ardkinglas. Count Victor, a foreigner, comes to a strange country and is pursued almost at once. The Baron of Doom and his castle give the tale its centre.

Chapters promise a spy wanted, an apparition, a lawyer's good lady, and a woman at a window. Mungo Boyd and chamberlain Sim MacTaggart serve the household as intrigue gathers. A duel on the sands, a cell in the fosse, and the Duke's ball carry the action. Munro, a Highland writer, sets romance and conspiracy in the Argyll he knew well.
21344-the-young-bridge-tender-or-ralph-n:
Arthur M. Winfield, who also wrote the Rover Boys books, opens with Ralph Nelson, only son of a widow. His father once kept the swing bridge between Westville and Eastport on Keniscot Lake. Ralph holds the bridge tender's job himself when a smash at the bridge starts the action. Squire Paget wants the property and moves against the family.

Chapters follow a missing bill, a runaway, a midnight crime, and Ralph out on bail before the robbery is cleared up. Percy, the squire's son, hears something that matters. Winfield wrote upward-struggle tales for boys in the Alger line: honest work, false suspicion, and a rise earned by pluck.
21449-with-axe-and-rifle:
A boy watches his Irish family make a home in the wild West in W. H. G. Kingston's With Axe and Rifle. His father liked the country so well that he went back to Ireland for his bride. The boy, his brother Dan, and small sister Kathleen grow up on the frontier.

Kingston shows the settlers' grind against weather, sickness, bad neighbours, and raids. A tutor called the Dominie and Dio, a runaway slave they shelter, stand close to the family. A wicked man named Bracher and a strange hunter who keeps saving them add drama. The tale ends in sudden, glad relief.
21577-peter-simple:
Peter Simple is the fool of his family, and the navy gets him, in Captain Marryat's novel of 1834. His father, a clergyman and a noble family's youngest son, holds a rich living. Custom, Peter jokes, offers the family's greatest fool to the country's naval greatness.

At fourteen Peter is packed off, first to a stockbroker and then to sea. His slow wits prove sharper than folk think, as cruises and captures pile up. The book was Marryat's fourth, and it fixed his fame for comic sea fiction. Friendship with the loyal O'Brien gives the tale much of its heart.
21616-the-ape-the-idiot-other-people:
W. C. Morrow gathers dark tales in The Ape, the Idiot and Other People, copyrighted in 1897. The stories first ran in Lippincott's Magazine and in San Francisco papers. A fourth edition, from 1910, is the copy given here.

One tale opens on an ape who has lived in a cage since childhood, with no memory of free forests. Others treat a plague hero, a monster-maker, and a game of honour. Absinthe, dungeons, and faithful amulets supply the props of these grim pieces. Morrow writes with a cold, exact hand that made him a master of the weird tale.
21692-the-pirate-city-an-algerine-tale:
R. M. Ballantyne sets The Pirate City in Algiers, in a tale of action about 1817. A dear little old lady in Sicily opens the tale, her mouth a study of smiles. Her wrinkles, Ballantyne says, are each a separate smile around it.

Her son Lucien is meant for the Church, by his father's dearest wish. Juliet, an adopted child, is promised to a convent by her uncle the abbot. Against those quiet plans stands the pirate city itself, and its defeat by the British Navy. Ballantyne mixes comic portraiture at home with Barbary fighting abroad.
21733-the-giant-of-the-north-pokings-rou:
Arctic seas call in this Ballantyne adventure, whose subtitle promises pokings round the Pole. Ballantyne had lived in the Canadian north as a young Hudson's Bay clerk, and ice country was his home ground as a writer. His tales of the far north drew on real cold, real hunger, and real travel by sledge and boat.

The giant of the title and the voyage toward the Pole drive the story's wonders. Strange sights, hard weather, and tall tales gather around the push into the frozen seas. Ballantyne mixes fact from polar travel with a boy's love of marvels. The result is a northern yarn in his fullest storyteller's voice, equal parts camp talk and adventure.
21837-monopolies-and-the-people:
Trusts and monopolies are put on trial in this 1889 study by Charles Whiting Baker, an editor of The Engineering News. Baker promises two things: a fair survey of monopolies in every industry, and a plain discussion of their causes, growth, evils, and remedies. He admits his list cannot name every powerful combination, yet holds that the broad facts deserve wide knowledge.

The book is dedicated to all who love truth, justice, and the rights of the whole people. It appeared as the great trusts were reshaping American business and politics. Baker writes as an engineer among lawyers: facts first, then judgment. For readers of the trust era, it is a clear contemporary map of the fight that led to antitrust law.
21975-the-barbadoes-girl-a-tale-for-youn:
An orphan girl from the West Indies joins an English family in Mrs. Hofland's The Barbadoes Girl, a tale for young people reissued at Boston in 1863. Mr. Harewood tells his wife and children that the daughter of a dead friend is coming from Barbados to live with them. The children pepper him with questions. Edmund is grave and studious at twelve, Charles lively at ten, and Ellen, eight, the mildest and most modest of all.

Bacon and Addison supply the mottoes: indulged passion makes bitter work for repentance. Hofland was a prolific writer of improving tales. Her new girl's temper and the family's patience drive the lesson home. The book teaches the management of feeling through a stranger in the house, in the firm Victorian manner.
22174-andrew-melville:
William Morison wrote this life of Andrew Melville for the Famous Scots series. Melville, scholar and church reformer, led Scotland's Presbyterians after Knox. The struggle from 1574 to 1688 to keep the Presbyterian system fills the book. Morison argues that the system's benefits to Scotland justify that struggle.

Melville defied kings, rebuilt universities, and suffered exile for the Kirk's freedom. His famous rebuke of James VI, calling him God's silly vassal, echoes through the story. Morison writes in the brisk, admiring style of the Famous Scots volumes. The book gives general readers a compact life of the second founder of Scottish Presbyterianism.
22185-sonnie-boy-s-people:
James B. Connolly, the Irish-American writer of sea stories, published Sonnie-Boy's People as a set of tales. Connolly knew Gloucester fishermen and harbour towns at first hand. In the title story, Marie Welkie watches a stranger from her veranda while keeping an eye on her nephew. His fine clothes and easy assurance disturb and amuse her; his kindness to the boy pleases her more.

The stories circle Sonnie-Boy, a child among sailors, fishermen, and shore folk. Connolly writes dialect and sea talk with a reporter's ear. Humour and pathos mix in his port scenes. The collection shows why Connolly was rated among the best American sea-story writers of his day.
22264-irish-books-and-irish-people:
Stephen Gwynn wrote Irish Books and Irish People as essays on his country's letters and life. Behind everything, Gwynn says, lies a great social change. Ownership of Ireland's land was passing from landlords to the men who tilled it. That transfer, he argues, literally unenslaved three-fourths of Ireland's people, though its links to the life of the mind are obscure and intangible.

His essays connect the land change to Ireland's literary revival. Books, writers, and readers all stand in the new Ireland's making. Gwynn, a nationalist member of Parliament and man of letters, writes as an insider. The volume captures the Irish revival's confidence in the years before the Great War.
22346-exile:
Exile is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its figures belong to a strange order of scholars in robes. One of them, Oktan, stands slightly under Kinton's height of five feet ten.

Oktan has a long, supple trunk and short, bowed legs. His short, thick arms are carried high before his chest. That build leaves Kinton feeling something is out of proportion. Robes hide part of the oddness from casual eyes. Such close body detail builds an alien presence without explanation. Readers meet exiles whose forms set them apart. The tale plays on difference, strangeness, and the unease of standing near it.
22399-the-fireside-picture-alphabet-or-h:
The Fireside Picture Alphabet mixes an alphabet book with humor and droll moral tales. Its back pages advertise the publisher's other wares for children. Miss Hattie's French Bedstead and Tom Thumb's Carriage appear there.

New toys in preparation are also promised to young buyers. A manual of cricket and baseball is offered by mail. Its plans show how to lay out grounds and form clubs. Marylebone Club rules for cricket are included in that manual. Baseball rules from several clubs appear alongside them. As a whole, the volume shows how children's books were sold. Pictures taught letters while advertisements sold the next purchase.
22763-suite-mentale:
Randall Garrett wrote Suite Mentale, a science fiction story about minds joined in a telepathic gestalt and the strain of sharing thoughts. The catalog record gives no year. Garrett, a prolific magazine writer, liked clever premises worked out with a light, ironic hand, and a mental suite, minds in sequence like music, is one of his neatest.

The sample is pure Garrett misdirection. A doctor gives his brief verdict, he may live. His audience is a group of men in conservative business suits, holding soft felt hats outside the door. Mallon's eyes stop on the tallest man's face. Nothing in the scene admits how strange the case behind the door has been. The story that follows thinks hard about what linked minds would do to privacy, guilt, and selfhood.
22827-patchwork-a-story-of-the-plain-peo:
Anna Balmer Myers set Patchwork, her 1920 story of the Plain People, among Pennsylvania's plain-dressing farm families. A perfect June morning opens the tale, with perfume from countless blossoms tempting everyone outdoors. Sunshine, blue sky, and lavish early summer set the scene before any conflict arrives.

Against that beauty, Myers works out the tensions of a strict, close community. Young people in plain dress face the pull of the wider world, its clothes, music, and freedoms. The patchwork of the title fits both the quilts of the region and the pieced-together lives on the page. Myers knew this world well, and her sympathy shows. The novel remains a warm, informed portrait of Pennsylvania Dutch country life.
22948-rival-pitchers-of-oakdale:
Morgan Scott opens Rival Pitchers of Oakdale, published in 1911, at noon on a sunny April day. Boys cluster on the Oakdale Academy steps at noon, talking nothing but baseball. The season is about to open, and Scott says the fever of the game already runs in their veins.

Two pitchers, one mound. The rivalry promised by the title drives this entry in Scott's Oakdale sports series, with school honor and a girl's opinion never far away. The books sold clean competition to boy readers, complete with coaching in both pitching and conduct. Period slang and period certainty fill the pages. As a record of how America taught sport to its sons, it is hard to beat.
23126-eric-or-little-by-little:
A boy counts the days in Eric, or Little by Little. A young boy capers and claps at the news. His parents come home within the week, the family will stay a short while, and then, at last, school begins for him.

Frederic William Farrar's school story follows Eric Williams through an English public school, where small surrenders to temptation accumulate, little by little, into ruin. Few Victorian novels were pressed on schoolboys so hard, or remembered so vividly, fondly and ruefully at once. Farrar, a clergyman and schoolmaster, wrote to warn, and his warning became a genre landmark. Modern readers meet the original of a hundred school stories, sermon and all, with its pathos fully intact.
23148-droozle:
A puppy snake stars in Droozle. The narrator traces Droozle to art school days and a grand tour. An unscheduled stop in the Coffin system introduced him to ballpoint snakes, Coffin Two's chief export. By liftoff, one small snake had become his traveling companion.

A pet from another planet, carried home in a traveler's luggage, gives the story its gentle engine. Art school, a grand tour, and interstellar stopovers blend in a future where tourism includes other worlds. Droozle himself, part souvenir and part companion, tests what his owner owes a creature bought as a curiosity. The tone stays light, the questions real. It is a small, fond piece of science fiction about pets and responsibility.
a-dog-s-tale: A faithful dog tells Mark Twain’s 1903 tale of human cruelty. Her sad and simple story accuses us all. It pleads against cruelty to animals. Deeply moving from start to finish, deeply moving, against cruelty.
a-horse-s-tale: Mark Twain's 1907 novel narrated by a horse, Soldier Boy, who serves in the Spanish-American War and loves a young girl. Part animal story, part anti-imperialist satire, it is Twain's oddest late work. Uneven but fascinating, with flashes of the old master's anger and humor.
a-jacobite-exile:
A Jacobite Exile is an 1894 adventure novel by G A Henty. Sir Marmaduke Carstairs is a Jacobite, a supporter of the exiled Stuart cause, and he is denounced as a plotter against King William. He and his son Charlie flee England for Sweden, where a very different war is being fought under King Charles the Twelfth.

Charlie joins the foreign legion in Swedish service and wins honor in several campaigns against the Poles and Russians. Henty folds the boy's exile into the great northern wars of the age, mixing real battles with a young soldier's rise. The novel gives readers both a Jacobite's grievance and a tour of Charles the Twelfth's battlefields.
a-modest-proposal-for-preventing-the-chi: Jonathan Swift's 1729 shocker: a calm, logical proposal that the Irish sell their children as food to the rich. The deadpan savagery makes it the most famous satire in English, a protest against English cruelty to Ireland disguised as economics. Short, horrifying, and brilliant.
a-prefect-s-uncle: Wodehouse's school farce introduces the prefect's alarming uncle — a former Oxford man whose unexpected arrival disrupts all order. Cricket, ragging, and comic chaos fill this early gem. Young Wodehouse already in glorious form. The result is schoolboy comedy of the most irresistible kind.
an-enemy-of-the-people: Ibsen's 1882 drama about Dr. Stockmann, who discovers the town's baths are poisoned and is declared an enemy for saying so. "The strongest man is he who stands alone." A timeless parable of truth versus the crowd, as relevant as ever.
armadale: Wilkie Collins's 1866 sensation novel: two Allan Armadales, a deadly inheritance, and the villainous Lydia Gwilt, one of fiction's great femme fatales. Intricate, thrilling, and long, it is Collins at his most elaborate. A masterpiece of Victorian suspense.
b09-sachs-fastnachtspiele:
Hans Sachs, the Nuremberg shoemaker and master singer, wrote plays for Shrove Tuesday, the carnival before Lent. Four of his Fastnachtspiele, carnival plays, are gathered here in German, from about 1550. The best known of them, Der fahrende Schüler im Paradies, sends a wandering scholar through a comic Paradise.
