The note states that articles about Gonzalez mention he was hiding behind a billboard in Dallas on November 22, 1963, the day President Kennedy was shot. Notes like this one were the researcher's raw material, a single reported fact about a single man, kept for whatever case it might one day join.
govdocs-archive_org-principles-of-counte: Chapter 5 of a work on counterdeception takes up deception in the global security environment. It lays out rules for counterdeception: how to spot lies told by rival states and how to answer them. Deception is an old tool of war and diplomacy, and the chapter treats it as a problem with methods, not mysteries. The author is not named in the record. Strategists and students of intelligence are its natural readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Long before the missiles arrived, Cuba spent two years asking Moscow for arms and protection. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, posted in November 2022 for the sixtieth anniversary of the Cuban Missile Crisis. It is the second part of a series on getting to know the Cubans.

From late 1960 into early 1961, Cuban-Soviet ties grew stronger month by month. Cuban leaders repeatedly requested military help and security guarantees from the Soviets. They voiced rising fear of an American attack. The records correct a common habit of telling 1962 as only a Washington-Moscow story.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cuba_A_Harsh_and_:
At the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, Fidel Castro wrote to Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev. He urged a course so extreme that the letter is still known by a grim label: the Armageddon letter. A National Security Archive news post from January 2018 presents that letter and the harsh and terrible solution it proposed.

Castro feared an American attack on Cuba was near, and his letter pushed Khrushchev toward striking first rather than waiting. Khrushchev refused, and the crisis ended with Soviet missiles withdrawn instead. Few single documents show the pressure leaders put on each other in those thirteen days so starkly. The posting gives readers the text's meaning in context: an ally's panic, a superpower's restraint, and how close the arguments came to the worst outcome.
green-short-history-english-people:
Green's Short History of the English People, in the 1883 printing, retold the national past for a vast public. Chaucer and the plowman share his stage with kings and queens. Social life comes first, where older histories put battles and courts alone.

The book sold in the hundreds of thousands and changed its trade. Green made history a story of the people's work, faith, and song. His vivid sketches of towns, fields, and workshops won readers everywhere. Critics praised its freshness while scholars used it for decades. It stands as the Victorian classic that opened English history to common readers.
greenmantle: Greenmantle, John Buchan's thriller. Another edition. This book preserves that novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
hawthorne-and-his-circle: Julian Hawthorne — the author's son — recalls his father Nathaniel and the great circle around him: Emerson, Longfellow, and the Concord luminaries. Intimate, affectionate, and full of literary gossip, it brings America's golden age vividly alive. A son's tribute and a biographer's treasure.
his-own-people: Young Tarkington sends rich Americans to Europe and watches the fun: dollars meet titles, and neither understands the other. Light, sharp, and good-natured, it is a comedy of the great American invasion. Tarkington’s Americans are as funny as they are recognizable.
j-cole: Emma Gellibrand's J. Cole tells an Australian story — the author's own country writ with local truth. Her colonial tales preserve a vanished world. A rare early Australian woman's voice. Bush stations and colonial society live in her lively, observant prose.
leonie-of-the-jungle:
Joan Conquest published her novel Leonie of the Jungle in New York in 1921. She had earlier written Desert Love. The Macaulay Company held the copyright that year.

Conquest dedicated the book to a native of India she calls splendid. Two books divide the tale: The West and The East. An epigraph quotes the line that East and West never meet. Leonie's story tests that claim through love and danger. Jungle settings and colonial romance drive Conquest's popular plot. Kipling's famous line frames her East-West romance. Conquest wrote many such colonial love stories for eager readers.
life-s-handicap-being-stories-of-mine-ow:
Rudyard Kipling gathers these stories of his own people in India. A 1915 printing carries his dedication dating the tales to 1887 and 1889. The preface describes a monastery called the Chubara of Dhunni Bhagat. Worn-out priests meditated in its gaily painted brick cells there.

Mango clumps, pipal trees, and tame parrots fill the courtyard. Hindu, Sikh, and Mahomedan mendicants rested together under its trees. One-eyed Gobind, a holy man, told Kipling the framing tale. Old men there found all creeds wonderfully alike and colourless. Parrots tore through the mango trees above brick-paved paths. Thousands of naked feet had worn those paths into gutters.
little-prudy-s-dotty-dimple:
Sophie May opens this children's book with Dotty's babyhood. Alice is the youngest of the Parlin family, readers learn. Grandma Read gathers the children into the kitchen. She tells them about their new little sister there.

Susy dances for joy at the news. Prudy falls down the cellar stairs in her delight. She rolls as softly as a pincushion, unhurt. Chapters promise verses, nestlings, parties, and a wedding to come. The bone man and Dotty's verses follow the babyhood chapter. Buying a brother and a wedding close her adventures. Fanny Harlow's party gives Dotty a social world beyond the nursery.
lord-arthur-savile:
Oscar Wilde made this set of short tales in 1891, in the same rich years as Dorian Gray. The title tale stands first, and three more tales stand by its side. Wilde's wit, so sharp in his plays, runs all through these prose tales too.

Lord Arthur Savile is told by a hand reader that he is fated to kill a man. In good faith, he sets out to get the deed done before his wedding day can come. 'The Canterville Ghost' turns the haunted house tale on its head, to great comic effect.
love-instigated-the-story-of-a-carved-iv:
Love Instigated is a slight gift-book tale by Douglass Sherley of Louisville, Kentucky. Its full title calls it the story of a carved ivory umbrella handle. The book was sold as a Christmas booklet in a box for one dollar. A de luxe edition, signed and limited to ninety-nine copies, cost ten.

Sherley also wrote The Story of a Picture, the adverts say. A companion tale, Love Perpetuated, tells the story of a dagger. The motto claims that the man who plants cabbages imitates God. Such dainty booklets were holiday gifts in the Gilded Age. This one survives as a curious piece of Louisville publishing.
lucile:
Lucile is a long verse novel by Owen Meredith, pen name of Edward Robert Bulwer Lytton. He dedicated the poem to his father, the famous novelist. A line from Hamlet stands at its head, about watching and sleeping. Meredith feared his new verse form had no footprints before it.

The poem tells of Lucile, a French lady of grace and sorrow. Two men love her, and her heart is torn between them. The tale moves through drawing rooms and across Europe's great events. Its smooth stanzas carried the story to a huge public. Lucile was the best-selling poem-novel of the Victorian age. Readers memorized its lines as they now memorize songs.
lulu-alice-and-jimmie-wibblewobble:
Lulu, Alice and Jimmie Wibblewobble is a children's book by Howard R. Garis. R. F. Fenno published it in New York in 1912, with colored pictures. It belongs to Garis's Bedtime Stories series for the very young. The Wibblewobbles are a family of ducks in his animal world.

Lulu and Alice are the sisters, and Jimmie is their brother. Short tales follow their small adventures, mishaps, and lessons. Garis wrote dozens of such animal books for children. His style is simple, warm, and full of gentle fun. The Wibblewobble stories sit beside his Littletail rabbit tales. They make easy reading for bedtime or first readers.
luther-bondage-of-the-will-cole:
Erasmus defended free will; Luther answered with The Bondage of the Will, the most uncompromising book he ever wrote. Henry Cole's English translation of 1823 carries the argument here. Luther himself ranked the treatise as his finest work, and scholars have argued about it ever since.

Human will, he claims, rides like a beast between God and Satan, unable to choose its rider. Only grace frees the captive will; nothing in us earns the rescue. The prose hits like a hammer, wit and fury mixed. Across the page stands Europe's greatest humanist, outmatched in sheer theological force. The debate over freedom and grace has never found a louder opening round.
mary-anerley-a-yorkshire-tale:
R. D. Blackmore published Mary Anerley, a Yorkshire tale, in 1880. The book opens far from any house, on a dreary moor road. That road drops to a swift river at Seven Corpse Ford.

Eight farmers once rode into that ford in fog and heavy rain. Seven drowned, and the place kept its grim name. Richard Yordas set stones and a chain there so their sons might cross safe, and worse news soon came. The Tees runs fast and can kill, Blackmore warns at length. Moor, ford, and hall give the tale its stark Yorkshire ground.
medieval-people:
Eileen Power wrote Medieval People, first printed in 1924. Power taught history at the University of London and at Girton College. Her preface defends a close, personal way of writing social history.

She says past lives live best when shown through one person at a time. As much proof can survive for a plain man as for a duke, she argues. Cloister and school, in a Langland quote, frame her world. The book rebuilds plain lives from records most histories pass by. Langland's Piers Plowman gives the book its front quote. Power's aim is the past made to live for plain readers.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
The Duke of Saint-Simon's memoirs appear here in a complete set. Fifteen volumes make up the whole work, by the contents list. Volume one opens with his birth, family, and early life.

He joins the Musketeers and marches to the siege of Namur. Dreadful weather, monks, and rival couriers fill that first campaign. Later heads treat the Duc de Chartres' wedding and the death of his father. The whole sweep runs from Louis XIV's court into the Regency years. Saint-Simon's eye for rank and slight fills each of the volumes. Few court lives of that age are told at such length.
memoirs-vieux-souvenirs-of-the-prince-de:
The Prince de Joinville's memoirs, Vieux Souvenirs, appear here in Lady Mary Loyd's English. Chapter one covers the years 1818 to 1830 of his life. He was born at Neuilly-sur-Seine on August 14, 1818.

A wet nurse took him at birth, as was the custom then. His first clear memory is a Twelfth Night dinner in 1824. Louis XVIII hosted the whole royal house at the Tuileries that night. Drums, guards, and the King's dinner passing on the stairs dazzled the boy. Talma on stage, in a gilt cuirass, struck the small boy too. A prince's childhood is shown through family rooms, not state halls.
moby-dick-or-the-whale:
Herman Melville published Moby-Dick at New York and London in 1851. He inscribed it to Nathaniel Hawthorne, in token of his admiration for Hawthorne's genius. The contents begin with Loomings, The Carpet Bag, and The Spouter-Inn. Ishmael, the narrator, signs aboard a Nantucket whaler after chapters on the town and its chowder.

Captain Ahab drives the Pequod after one white whale, Moby Dick. Melville mixes the hunt with whaling lore, sermons, and metaphysics. The book sold poorly in his lifetime and was rediscovered in the twentieth century. It now stands as the great American novel of obsession, labor, and the sea.
monitress-merle:
Angela Brazil wrote this girls' school story as a sequel by request. She dedicates it to readers who asked for the further adventures of Mavis and Merle. Treyer Evans illustrated the volume. The contents open with a last bathe and a school ballot. Merle becomes the new monitress of her school at Chagmouth.

The seaside setting brings fishermaidens, a ferry, and a boat called The Kittiwake. School episodes include the mumps, a performance facing the footlights, and fifth form justice. A haunted tree and Yuletide close the list. Brazil practically invented the modern school story, and her boarding-school world runs on friendship, scrapes, and honor.
mr-bingle:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote this novel, illustrated by James Montgomery Flagg. McCutcheon was known for Graustark and The Prince of Graustark. The contents open with the five little Sykeses and an odd relation. The death of Uncle Joe follows, and the story of Joseph. Thomas Singleton Bingle earns the title Honorable midway through.

Later chapters treat the affairs of Amy and Dick, and Mr. Bingle thinking of becoming an angel. Trouble triples, the law speaks its last word, and December brings another Christmas Eve. The opening scene warms the Bingle apartment in lower New York with a coal fire, since the steam pipes refuse to heat.
my-beautiful-lady-nelly-dale:
Thomas Woolner, a noted sculptor, wrote this tale in verse and prose. Cassell issued the 1887 edition in London, Paris, and New York. Its heroine is Nelly Dale, the beautiful lady of the title. An introduction praises Woolner's song of noble earthly love.

The intro frames love as a spur to high endeavor. Duty speaks like a call to war in its lines. The book joins a library built on belief in human worth. Milton is quoted on books that hold a potency of life. Woolner's tale is earnest Victorian romance, aiming to lift hearts by showing love that makes men strive.
my-neighbors-stories-of-the-welsh-people:
Caradoc Evans tells stories of the Welsh people in this 1920 book. Harcourt, Brace and Howe issued it in New York. Evans dedicated it to Thomas Burke of Limehouse Nights. An opening essay, The Welsh People, sets the tone.

He calls God a big man, taller than the highest chapel. Tales named Love and Hate and The Two Apostles follow. Treasure, widows, and unanswered prayers fill the contents. Evans writes of chapel folk with a hard, comic edge. His Welsh neighbors scheme, pray, and grasp in small villages. The book shocked some readers and made Evans the bold voice of Welsh fiction.
my-tropic-isle:
E. J. Banfield, famed as the beachcomber of Dunk Island, wrote this island book. Fisher Unwin issued it in London in 1911. Much of it first ran in the North Queensland Register as Rural Homilies. Banfield thanks museum men in Sydney for help naming specimens.

Two lines from Milton front the book, praising the wilderness. Banfield lived simply on a Great Barrier Reef isle. He writes of birds, reefs, weather, and his Aboriginal neighbors. V1 calls the result gentle natural history and an Australian classic. Turtles, shells, and bright birds fill a calm record of a man who chose the tropic shore.
nasa-tm-19630002674-cold-air-investigati:
John E. McAulay of Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-42, in September 1959. It reports cold-air tests of three rocket nozzles. Each nozzle can change the size of its throat, the narrow waist of the nozzle. The shape is called convergent-divergent, since it squeezes then flares.

Changing the throat lets a crew throttle thrust up or down. Cold flow tests use plain air, not hot exhaust, for safety and ease. McAulay measured how each design behaved across its range. Such data guided nozzles for engines that must vary their push, a key need for advanced rockets and jets.
nasa-tm-19650012052-ibm-7094-program-for:
Henry Miller at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this program description for the IBM 7094 computer. The program solves what the title calls the six-coil problem. It was written in Fortran, the standard language for scientific computing at the time. Goddard document X-543-64-366 covers the program.

Miller sets out what the program does and how it is organized. Program descriptions let other users run and trust a code without reading every line. They also let later staff maintain it. In 1964, a shared program like this one saved each new user from starting over.
nasa-tm-19680017759-are-gas-core-nuclear:
Robert G. Ragsdale of Lewis Research Center asks whether gas-core nuclear rockets can actually be built in this 1968 conference paper. In such an engine, gaseous nuclear fuel sits at the center of a cavity. Hydrogen propellant flows around the fuel and carries away fission heat as thermal radiation.

Ragsdale reduces engine needs to two key parameters. One is the share of cavity volume filled by gaseous fuel. The other is the ratio of hydrogen flow to uranium flow through the engine. He builds an engine performance map from those two values. Available experimental data are then placed on the map. The map lets engineers judge this concept against rivals fairly.
nasa-tm-19680026660-performance-of-a-col:
Robert A. Wasko and Douglas E. Harrington of Lewis Research Center tested a collapsible plug nozzle with two shroud designs in this 1968 report. One shroud was a two-position cylindrical type. The other was a variable angle floating shroud. Tests ran from rest up to Mach 2.0 flight conditions.

At subsonic cruise, both shrouds performed nearly the same. The two-position shroud did better during subsonic acceleration. The floating shroud did better at supersonic Mach numbers. External flow effects peaked at Mach 1.2 for both configurations. Static performance was measured across a wide range of nozzle pressure ratios. The study guides shroud choice for plug nozzle engines.
nasa-tm-19710002949-us-patents-for-nasa-:
NASA issued this catalog of United States patents for its own inventions. The patents listed are open for licensing inside the United States. Several thousand inventions, the introduction notes, result each year from NASA-supported research, covering nearly every field of technology, and many carry real commercial value.

Inventions with government importance or strong commercial promise are the ones NASA patents. To spread their use, the agency offers nonexclusive, royalty-free licenses for the life of a patent. If no commercial use appears within two years, an exclusive license may go to a qualified applicant instead. The catalog gives the application steps and the Washington office where inquiries were to be sent.
nasa-tm-19710009153-nuclear-power-for-su:
Frank E Rom of the Lewis Research Center wrote this technical paper on nuclear power for giant surface effect vehicles and aircraft. Rom presented early results from a cost study of very large nuclear craft built to haul cargo across oceans. Surface effect vehicles ride on a cushion of air just above the water.

The study found such craft might move cargo for one to two cents per ton mile. Moving all cargo worth shipping at that rate would take about fifteen hundred huge surface craft, or five hundred huge aircraft. Rom also reported reactor impact tests. Test reactors survived hits at high speed against reinforced concrete without leaking.
nasa-tm-19710011714-preliminary-results-:
Martin U Gutstein of the Lewis Research Center and James A Bond of General Electric reported these boiler tests in March 1971. The hardware was a single tube potassium boiler for the advanced Rankine system. That system was a planned nuclear electric power plant for space. Lithium heated the tube, and potassium boiled inside it.

Exit steam heat reached as high as fourteen hundred twenty kelvin. The report gives the heat pattern inside the boiler. It also gives pressure losses at varied potassium flow rates. Boiling heat transfer values cover a range of exit dryness and superheat. One test mimicked plant startup. The team called the test success a major step for hot liquid metal power systems.
nasa-tm-19710019491-compact-30-kw-circul:
G. E. McDonald, H. A. Putre, M. C. Swanson, and P. M. Finnegan of the Lewis Research Center wrote this memorandum, NASA TM X-52676, with L. Homyak of the Plum Brook Station. It describes a compact capsule that circulates helium to cool nuclear fuel specimens during tests. The capsule was built for work inside the NASA Plum Brook Reactor.

One capsule was endurance tested outside the reactor, and two more were run inside it. The abstract lists demonstrated performance: high pressures, wall temperatures, and specimen powers up to the capsule's thirty-kilowatt rating. The design uses a motor-driven vane pump, a concentric tube heat exchanger, and a fuel test section made from modified commercial parts. The authors note that a loss-of-coolant accident could be contained without shutting the reactor down, and that spent capsules are cheap enough to discard.
nasa-tm-19720013351-peak-axial-velocity-:
D E Groesbeck, U H von Glahn, and R G Huff of the Lewis Research Center studied jet noise in March 1972, as NASA TM X-68047. Their concern was the externally blown flap, a lift system for short takeoff aircraft. Engine jets strike the lowered flaps and gain lift. That striking also creates an unacceptable rise in noise. Lowering the jet speed before impact is the known cure.

The speed must fall within a set distance behind the nozzle. Multi element nozzles promise that faster decay of peak jet speed. The team compared rectangular and triangular nozzle shapes for the job. Their measurements tracked how fast the centerline velocity dropped. Quieter short field aircraft depended on exactly this trade. The study fed the broader quiet STOL research effort.
nasa-tm-19720016558-a-bibliographical-su:
William R Corliss prepared this bibliography on January 15, 1970, for NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It surveys writing on large scale systems and their control. Large scale systems range from power grids to whole cities. Controlling them was a young field with scattered literature. Corliss gathered that literature into one partly annotated list. The foreword frames the work as serving a better quality of life.

About four hundred references fill the survey. They are sorted into thirteen application areas. Large societal systems and large communication systems are among them. Short notes mark the value of key entries. A first author index closes the volume. The survey runs to about one hundred fifty pages.
parkman-la-salle:
La Salle and the Discovery of the Great West came out in 1869. Parkman made it Part Three of France and England in North America. The French explorer's descent of the Mississippi drives the whole book.

La Salle claims the river's mouth and the Gulf for France. Mutiny, hunger, and vast wild lands test him at every stage. His triumph ends in murder by his own weary men. Parkman tells the tale as high romance grounded in hard records. Many call it the most stirring story in early American history and exploration. La Salle's drive and doom grip readers to the end.
patriotic-plays-and-pageants-for-young-p: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Patriotic Plays and Pageants for Young People, the publisher's catalogue pages, title page, and copyright notice of 1912, with no play text visible. The catalogue describes Constance D'Arcy Mackay's one-act plays as dealing with the youth of American heroes, meant for schools, camps, and clubs. They can be used singly or linked into indoor or outdoor pageants, with directions for costumes, dances, and music.
peter-simple:
Captain Frederick Marryat's Peter Simple, dated 1834 in this record, is narrated by Peter himself. He calls himself the fool of the family, and by the old custom the greatest fool is sacrificed to the navy. At fourteen, having dreamed of a tailor's comfortable shopboard, he is chosen by general acclamation of his aunts and cousins.

His clergyman father sends him to London on the outside of the coach, booked in the way-bill like a parcel, carriage paid. Delivered to a stockbroker's house in St. Clement's Lane, Peter begins the midshipman's life that made the novel a classic of the sea.
podcast-dannyjones-ZRddaJfdalE:
Ed Barnhart and Luke Caverns join Danny Jones to talk about a lost Maya city in North America. The episode title calls it a super city found by an archaeologist. Barnhart is a scholar of Maya sites, and Caverns studies old sites in the field.

The guests describe the finds, the scale of the ruins, and why the site may change what we know of Maya reach. They also explain how new scans from the air helped spot the city under thick growth. Jones asks what the team plans to dig next. Listeners get a ground level view of a find that could redraw old maps.
podcast-joerogan-Uc5_z6buSLE:
Researcher Jimmy Corsetti shares new evidence for the Atlantis theory in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Corsetti, of the Bright Insight channel, argues that Plato's lost island matches a real site in the Sahara, the Richat Structure. His case has a large online following.

He walks Rogan through the rings of the Eye of the Sahara and how they echo Plato's account of rings of land and water. Rogan asks what would settle the claim and why experts resist it. The segment is a focused brief for one bold idea, delivered by its best-known advocate.
podcast-tuckercarlson-0aLXZj-oBLE:
Tucker Carlson addresses a packed Charlie Kirk event on the Epstein case. He jokes about the wild walkout music and the huge crowd. Then he turns to what others said that night.

Carlson says he watched a rival host's take the day before. He offers a different view of the cover-up charge. The title calls the speech his message to America. He argues the case reveals how power guards itself. The tape preserves a live address to loyal fans who demanded answers their leaders would not give. He speaks as both friend and fellow fighter.
podcast-tuckercarlson-XrJUczTBILE:
Our airspace is being invaded, Carlson warns in a segment of Tucker Carlson's podcast, taking up the drone sightings that alarmed the country. Strange craft were reported over bases and coasts, and officials offered few clear answers. Carlson treats the silence as part of the story.

He reviews the sightings and the government's shifting statements, and asks why the world's best-funded military cannot say what flies over its own bases. The talk speaks to a wider public unease about control of the skies. The segment is a dated record of that scare, in the host's own alarmed and pointed style.
podcast-tuckercarlson-ykBp1WhdfLE:
Tucker Carlson speaks in a solo talk on what he calls Donald Trump's desecration of Easter. The title adds a warning to Christians in all lands. Carlson frames the charge as a man of faith, not just a host.

Carlson lays out the acts he says made the holy day a stage for pride and spite. He warns that faith bent to a man's brand will rot from within. He calls on Christians to hold their creed above any king or chief. Listeners get a stern sermon from a host to his own side. The library keeps the talk as a record of his stated view.
richard-hannay-02-greenmantle:
John Buchan's Greenmantle, dated 1916 in its heading, sends Richard Hannay back to secret war work. A dedication to Caroline Grosvenor says the tale was scribbled in odd places and moments over the past year. Buchan warns readers not to call its events improbable, for the war has driven that word out of use.

The dedication reports the cast: Sandy last heard of at Basra, Blenkiron cured and home in the States, and Peter in the Flying Corps. Chapter one finds Hannay convalescing at Furling in Hampshire after Loos. A telegram from Bullivant arrives as Sandy hunts the marmalade, and Hannay wonders why the Foreign Office wants an obscure major in double-quick time.
robinson-crusoe-in-words-of-one-syllable:
Mary Godolphin retold Defoe's Robinson Crusoe in words of one syllable, for the youngest readers. Her preface says the title explains the book, and her task was chiefly to reduce the common language to short words. Only the names Xury and Friday, and the titles of the pictures, break the rule.

One-syllable books of the day, she notes, offered little more than a few short, unlinked sentences in spelling books. She offers a whole famed story instead. It opens with Crusoe born at York, longing for the sea from childhood. He breaks loose from school and home, walks to Hull, and ships out, meeting a squall, a leak, and the pumps within days.
same-old-bill-eh-mable: Edward Streeter, of the 27th (N.Y.) Division, wrote Same Old Bill, Eh Mable, with twenty-seven black-and-white pictures by G. William Breck, also of the 27th Division, issued in New York in 1919. Streeter is named as author of Dere Mable and Thats Me All Over, Mable. The front pages also mark a cover page picture at the head of the list.
sergeant-york-and-his-people: A transcriber's note frames this book as a close, dramatic portrait of an ideal American soldier: thoughtful, brave, modest, kind, and loyal. The note pairs the book with a broad history of the World War, which it complements with a personal view. The pages at hand hold that note plus a glossary of hard words, with entries from light banter to land-bound terms. No chapter text or author's name appears in these opening pages, so the soldier's story itself cannot be told from what is shown here.
siege-of-washington-d-c-written-expressl:
Capt. F. Colburn Adams wrote this mock-heroic account of the siege of Washington for young readers, issued in New York in 1867. Adams had written The Story of a Trooper before this. A preface reports his publisher's fear that generals will take offense at the artist's liberties with their dignity.

Adams answers that great generals will laugh, while little ones were always fiercer against writers than against the enemy. He calls the siege the most remarkable military event in history, with tongue in cheek. Children of the Civil War era got war news as satire, aimed at pomp and panic in the capital.
sir-john-oldcastle:
The True and Honorable History of the Life of Sir John Oldcastle, the Good Lord Cobham, stands here as a play ascribed in part to William Shakespeare. A cast list crowds kings, lords, judges, bishops, rebels, and Lady Cobham around Henry the Fifth. The prologue speaks first to clear the hero's name.

No pampered glutton stands here, the prologue insists, answering those who knew Oldcastle as a stage fat knight. The true Cobham was a Lollard lord tried for heresy and hanged as a traitor. This old play gives the grave counter-tale: a faithful, wronged knight rather than a tavern joke.
stories-of-the-prophets-before-the-exile:
Isaac Landman wrote Stories of the Prophets (Before the Exile) for the Commission on Jewish Education of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations and the Central Conference of American Rabbis. Landman dedicated the book to his parents, who first brought him to the prophets.

The contents begin with The Shepherd of Tekoah, the prophet Amos, in chapters called An End to War, In the Days of Prosperity, and The Man Who Dared. The book retells the lives and messages of the early prophets as stories for young Jewish readers, stressing courage and justice. It was made as teaching material for religious schools, with a named board of rabbis and educators behind it.
style:
Walter Raleigh's Style, in its fifth impression from Edward Arnold at London in 1904, is a short essay on how English prose is written well. Raleigh had already written The English Novel and a critical essay on Robert Louis Stevenson, and he dedicates the little book, in Latin, to John Sampson, a librarian friend and fellow traveller.

A table of principal matters maps the argument, which treats the choice of words, the building of sentences, and the difference between writing that lives and writing that merely fills pages. Raleigh argues for clearness, force, and music in prose, and against fine writing that shows off. The essay became a standard pocket guide for students of English.
swingin-round-the-cirkle:
Petroleum V. Nasby, the pen name of David Ross Locke, published Swingin Round the Cirkle at Boston through Lee and Shepard in 1867, with illustrations by Thomas Nast. The book collects his letters to the public press during 1866, written as the semi-literate pastor of the Church of the New Dispensation and postmaster at Confederate Cross Roads, Kentucky.

Nasby's mock dedication addresses Androo Johnson, the pride and hope of Dimocrisy, who had swung around the entire circle of official honor from alderman to president. The letters, in thick dialect spelling, satirize President Johnson's famous Swing Around the Circle tour and the politics of Reconstruction, letting a foolish copperhead preacher damn his own cause with every sentence.
tarzan-the-terrible:
Edgar Rice Burroughs set Tarzan the Terrible in a hidden land of beast-men, with twenty-five chapters and a word list at the close. Chapter heads name strange peoples and beasts, from the Pithecanthropus and the Tor-o-don to the gryf and the city A-lur.

The opening stalks a great cat through a midnight jungle, silent on twigs and leaves, eyes round in the dark. That hunt sets the tone for a land where men with tails, temple rites, and blood-stained altars wait. Tarzan must cross pits, lion dens, and a forbidden garden to find what he seeks. Readers get one of the wildest of the Tarzan quests.
temple-trouble:
H. Beam Piper wrote Temple Trouble as a science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction, where it ran in April 1951. A head note sums the plot: time travelers plant fake wonders to win mining rights, but nature and men can plant counter-wonders too.

The tale opens through incense and altar smoke, where the idol Yat-Zar glares from a gold throne in a vast pillared temple. He bears three turquoise eyes, six arms, a gold-wire beard, and bird's feet, holding sword, torch, goblet, and scales. Readers get Piper's paratime world at work, where agents pose as gods and a staged faith starts to slip from their grip.
the-adventure-of-the-red-circle:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote The Adventure of the Red Circle as a Sherlock Holmes tale, told by Dr. Watson. It opens in the Baker Street rooms, where Holmes tries to brush off a landlady's plea and turn back to his scrapbook.

Mrs. Warren holds her ground with a landlady's grit and guile. She reminds Holmes that he once cleared up a case for her lodger Mr. Fairdale Hobbs, who never stopped praising his kindness. Soft words and a true debt of thanks move Holmes to sigh, lay down his gum brush, and hear her out. Readers get a case of a secret lodger, coded lamp signals, and an Italian vendetta worked out on London streets.
the-adventures-of-jimmie-dale: Frank L. Packard wrote The Adventures of Jimmie Dale, a crime tale. It splits into two parts. Part One is The Man in the Case. Part Two is The Woman in the Case. Chapters for the first part start with The Gray Seal. The Mother Lode and The Counterfeit Five follow. Devil's Work and The Man Higher Up come later. The second part brings The Crime Club. The Innocent Bystander and The Tocsin stand in that part.
the-adventures-of-peregrine-pickle:
Tobias Smollett wrote The Adventures of Peregrine Pickle, a novel in which are included the Memoirs of a Lady of Quality. This first volume opens with an account of Mr. Gamaliel Pickle and the temper of his sister.

Gamaliel Pickle lives in a county of England bounded by the sea, a hundred miles from the capital. His father, a London merchant, rose from small starts to high honors in the city and a plump fortune. Yet he died, to his deep regret, just short of a plum — falling shy of his goal by less than fifteen thousand pounds. His dying charge bids his son copy his thrift till the gap is filled. Readers then follow young Peregrine through school, sea, and scams, in Smollett's broad, biting picaresque.
the-age-of-fable:
Thomas Bulfinch wrote The Age of Fable. It is the first part of Bulfinch's Mythology. This copy binds it in a complete one-volume set. The Age of Chivalry and Legends of Charlemagne stand with it. A note warns that the copy holds the Fable part alone. A publishers' preface fronts the work.

That preface ranks The Age of Fable with a famed set. Pilgrim's Progress, Gulliver's Travels, and The Arabian Nights are named. Robinson Crusoe is named as well. The book is called a work each reader must know. Some part of it is a must before an education can be called complete. It is also called a monument to Bulfinch's wide learning and care. Readers get Greek and Roman myths retold in clear prose. The book stayed the standard English guide to the old gods for more than a century.
the-auchensaugh-renovation-of-the-nation:
Renewed at Auchensaugh, near Douglas, on July 24, 1712, the National Covenant and Solemn League and Covenant are printed here with an acknowledgment of sins and a pledge to duties. A Philadelphia edition of 1880 sets that deed beside the Paisley edition of 1820 and the Belfast edition of 1835. It also prints a later renewal ordered at Philadelphia on October 8, 1880, by the Reformed Presbytery.

A long preface defends the 1712 act as the one faithful renewal of the covenants. Its writers argue that opponents first attacked this deed, removed it from terms of communion, and in Scotland struck it out in 1822. Readers get both the old church pledges and a sharp case for keeping them unchanged.
the-autocrat-of-the-breakfast-table: Oliver Wendell Holmes's famous series of witty breakfast-table monologues, first published in The Atlantic Monthly in 1857. The Autocrat holds forth on everything from poetry and science to human nature, in essays that blend humor, philosophy, and good talk. They made Holmes America's most beloved man of letters and invented a whole style of familiar essay.
the-babylonian-story-of-the-deluge-as-to:
E. A. Wallis Budge retells the Babylonian flood story from Assyrian tablets found at Nineveh. He begins with Layard's digs in 1845 to 1847 and again in 1849 to 1851. The ruins lie across the Tigris from Mosul, on a site long linked by local and religious tradition to the ancient city.

Budge describes mounds, walls, and palaces built by kings such as Sargon II, Sennacherib, and Esarhaddon. One mound holds the palace and library of Ashur-bani-pal. Setting the scene in this detail lets readers see where the tablets lay before he turns to what the flood text itself says.
the-beast-in-the-jungle:
Henry James's tale, in a Martin Secker edition of 1915, opens at Weatherend, a great house shown to luncheon guests. John Marcher wanders through rooms full of pictures, heirlooms, and treasures, feeling pressed by their poetry and history. Among the visitors he meets May Bartram again.

Her face troubles him pleasantly, like the sequel to something whose start he has lost. She, by contrast, seems not to have lost the thread of their earlier meeting. That uneven memory drives the opening chapter. Marcher senses a shared past and a secret between them, while James lingers over glances, rooms, and half-formed feeling.
the-beetle:
Richard Marsh wrote this horror tale of an Egyptian beetle curse in 1897. It came out the same year as Dracula, and in its first year it sold more than Stoker's book. Marsh was a brisk hand at tales of dread for the broad public of his day.

A shape shifting being, part man, part woman, part beast, comes to London from Egypt. It seeks revenge on a young man of Parliament for a wrong done in a past age. The book caught the pulp dread of the 1890s in its most pure and wild form.
the-book-of-art-for-young-people: Agnes Ethel Conway and Sir Martin Conway wrote The Book of Art for Young People, put out in London by A. and C. Black. The book has sixteen full-page plates in color. It first came out in September 1909 as The Children's Book of Art, and was put out again in 1914, 1927, and 1935. The front plate is Red Riding Hood, from a work by G. F. Watts in the Birmingham Art Gallery. A note thanks lords, a herald, and friends for leave to use works and verse.
the-boy-ranchers-on-the-trail-or-the-dia: Willard F. Baker wrote The Boy Ranchers on the Trail, or The Diamond X After Cattle Rustlers. The chapter list starts with The Round-Up and A Curious Instrument. Startling News, The Scratched Safe, and The Broken Bottle come next. Then come Missing Steers, Four Eyes, and Throwing the Rope. A fire, hard questions, and a watch tower crowd the mid heads. The Signal and Four Eyes-No Eyes lead to A Big Raid, On the Trail, and Wild Country. The Boiling Spring is the last head shown.
the-bravo-a-tale:
J. Fenimore Cooper opens The Bravo: A Tale, in a form dated 1872, with a preface on how ill the world sorts its state terms. States are called monarchies or republics, he says, but each name hides wild splits.

Cooper says his aim was to give his own folk a picture of the social system of one of the so-called republics of the old world. He made no try at true men of the past in their grave dress. He set out the day-to-day work of Venetian state craft, and points to the known work of M. Daru for proof of the likeness. The preface then weighs how freedom grew in Europe, right by right won from rulers. That, he says, splits from the American rule, where the folk grant rights to the state.
the-bronze-eagle: Baroness Orczy wrote The Bronze Eagle: A Story of the Hundred Days, put out in New York by the George H. Doran Company with rights dated 1915. Orczy had also written The Laughing Cavalier and The Scarlet Pimpernel. A list of her books stands in front, naming A Bride of the Plains, El Dorado, Meadowsweet, The Noble Rogue, and Petticoat Rule. The subtitle alone sets the scene: the Hundred Days, Napoleon's last return to power. Only the front pages are shown, with no page of the tale itself.
the-campaign-of-chancellorsville: The Campaign of Chancellorsville, by Theodore A. Dodge, is dedicated to the Military Historical Society of Massachusetts, and its opening pages give the table of contents alone. Twenty-eight chapters and more are headed. They move from Hooker's appointment and the Army of Northern Virginia to the cavalry raid against Lee's communications. Jackson's march and attack, the Eleventh Corps, Fairview, and Sedgwick's operations follow. No narrative page is shown.
the-campaigns-of-the-british-army-at-was:
The Campaigns of the British Army at Washington and New Orleans, by G. R. Gleig, chaplain-general to the forces, appears here in a new edition dated 1879. Its advertisement insists the work is the only connected and authentic account of those expeditions. It is not a loose relation of hearsay. It was compiled from a journal kept during the progress of the events it describes.

The campaigns belong to the close of the late American war. The contents begin with the embarkation of the troops and their passage. Then comes the march to Bordeaux, before the history turns toward America. The claim the edition stakes is documentary: a connected history of two famous expeditions, written from notes made on the spot while the events were still unfolding.
the-choir-invisible: James Lane Allen wrote this novel, issued as a Project Gutenberg text in September 2000. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and release dates, plus a line crediting Susan L. Farley as transcriber.The book itself never opens here. The header is dated September 2000 and numbered 2316 in the Gutenberg series.
the-clue-of-the-twisted-candle:
Edgar Wallace opens this thriller with a delayed train and a wet walk. The 4.15 from Victoria to Lewes has been held at Three Bridges by a derailment. John Lexman catches a late connection to Beston Tracey, but the wagonette that links the village with the outside world has already gone.

The station-master offers to telephone the village and have Briggs come down in half an hour. Lexman looks at the dripping landscape, shrugs, and says he will walk. He leaves his bag at the station, buttons his mackintosh to his chin, and sets out into the rain for Little Tracey, two miles off. The downpour looks set to last all night, and the high hedges run like leafy cascades. He stops under a big tree to light his pipe, bowl turned down, and walks on. Wallace sets his man alone in foul weather before the candle clue appears.
the-court-of-boyville: William Allen White, author of The Real Issue, wrote The Court of Boyville, dated 1898, with pictures by Orson Lowell and, for the first story, Gustav Verbeek. Its contents list a prologue and tales such as The Martyrdom of Mealy Jones, A Recent Confederate Victory, James Sears: A Naughty Person, and The Herb Called Hearts-Ease. A short verse asks where Boyville lies and how a traveler might find the road back to its shady rows of corn. Only the front matter and contents are present here.
the-cruise-of-the-cachalot-round-the-wor:
Frank T. Bullen, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society who sailed as first mate, wrote The Cruise of the Cachalot about a round-the-world hunt for sperm whales. He dedicates the book to Miss Emily Hensley, in thanks for thirty years of friendship and practical help, calling himself her humble pupil.

In his preface Bullen claims a first: a cruise of a South Sea whaler told from the seaman's standpoint. Two older books on the subject, by ships' surgeons F. Debell Bennett and Thomas Beale, were written for science and have long been out of print, though Beale's stays the standard work on the sperm whale. Bullen aims at the general reader instead, setting out the methods and dangers of a calling the public knows nothing about, from his own observation and never at second hand.
the-devil-s-disciple:
George Bernard Shaw's The Devil's Disciple is a play in three acts. Act I opens in 1777 at the bleakest hour before a wintry dawn. Mrs. Dudgeon of New Hampshire sits up in the kitchen and general dwelling room of her farmhouse on the outskirts of Websterbridge.

The stage directions paint her as no prepossessing woman. Her face is cut deep by the barren forms of a dead Puritanism, which have soured her temper and hardened her pride. She has worked hard and gained only dominion and detestation in her sordid home. She also has an unquestioned name for piety and respectability among neighbors, to whom drink still tempts more than religion. They conceive goodness simply as self-denial.
the-discovery-of-the-source-of-the-nile:
John Hanning Speke wrote The Discovery of the Source of the Nile. A page of facts at the front records that Speke, born in 1827, served in the Punjab, left in 1854 to explore Somaliland. He found Lake Tanganyika with Burton and Lake Victoria on his own, and, with Grant, was the first European to cross equatorial Africa; he died in 1864.

An editor's note adds that Speke was thirty-six when his Nile journal appeared. He had entered the army in 1844 and served ten years in India, through the Punjab campaign, already dreaming of African exploration. He joined the expedition then preparing under Lieutenant Burton for the Somali country, was wounded by the Somalis. He came home on sick leave as the Crimean War broke out, serving through it before joining another expedition in December 1856.
the-elder-brother-the-works-of-francis-b: The Elder Brother heads a volume of plays by Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher. Their life years head the page: 1584 to 1616, and 1579 to 1625. Arnold Glover and A. R. Waller edited the text for Cambridge University Press in 1906. The volume also holds The Spanish Curate, Wit Without Money, and Beggars Bush. Only the title matter and contents are present here. No scene from any play follows.
the-enchanted-castle:
Margaret Ostler receives the dedication of The Enchanted Castle, dated September 1907 from Soho. In verse, E Nesbit thanks Peggy for bringing the airs of heath and moor through her door. Chapter one names the three children. Gerald is called Jerry. James is called Jimmy. Kathleen is Cathy, or Puss Cat, to her brothers.

The three board at schools in a small western town, boys apart from girls. Holidays lead them to a great house with a magic ring and stone beasts that stir. Nesbit blends plain child talk with true wonder.
the-evil-eye-or-the-black-spector-the-wo:
William Carleton's The Evil Eye; or, The Black Spector opens with a short preface on its theme. The belief in the evil eye, Carleton says, has spread to every land on earth, and in his own youth it stood as settled dogma. Yet schooling and knowledge are wearing it thin, he notes, and soon such idle faiths will fade.

Some lore he traces to the Druids, whom he respects save for tales of human sacrifice. His tale then shows the blight at work in Irish farm life: envy, curses, and fear. Carleton writes from inside the world he shows.
the-fool-errant-being-the-memoirs-of-fra:
Maurice Hewlett framed The Fool Errant as the memoirs of Francis-Antony Strelley, a citizen of Lucca, and gives himself the role of editor. The book came out in July 1905, given to J. M. Barrie.

Strelley tells his own tale in the first person: a plea for his acts, a love for Aurelia, a fall, and a road taken as a pilgrim. He meets a pedlar of crosses, falls in with Fra Palamone, is held in bondage, and quarrels and makes up with Virginia. Hewlett builds a bright, old-world tale of love, pride, and a fool's slow schooling in Italy.
the-framework-of-home-rule:
Erskine Childers wrote The Framework of Home Rule in 1911 to set out how Ireland might rule itself. Childers was known for The Riddle of the Sands and for works on cavalry and war.

His chapters trace Ireland and America side by side: settlement, revolt, Grattan's Parliament, and the Union. He then sets Canada, Australia, and South Africa next to Ireland, drawing the points of likeness before he states Ireland's case as it stood in his day. The last chapter builds the frame itself: the parts of the problem and the shape of a home rule law that could hold both Irish claims and the tie to Britain.
the-further-adventures-of-jimmie-dale: Frank L. Packard wrote The Further Adventures of Jimmie Dale as tales of a rich man who robs as the Gray Seal, printed in 1919. Only the front matter and contents are present here. The heads name Smarlinghue, a man with a scar, a diamond pendant, cries of death to the Gray Seal, a bond robbery, voices of the underworld, a sanctuary, and a secret room. No chapter text shows up in these pages, so the capers cannot be told from these opening pages alone.
the-great-doctrines-of-the-bible: Rev. William Evans wrote The Great Doctrines of the Bible. The book grew out of classroom lectures, set in lasting form at his students' request. Only the front matter and foreword are present here. The contents list doctrines of God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit, then of man, the church, the Scriptures, angels, and Satan. Salvation covers repentance, faith, regeneration, justification, adoption, sanctification, and prayer. The last things cover the Second Coming, the Judgment, and the reward of the righteous. His method, he says, is Biblical, not dogmatic.
the-greylock-a-fairy-tale:
Georg Ebers wrote The Greylock, a fairy tale. Long ago stood a land fairer than any other. Beside a lake of deepest blue lay the castle of the Duke who ruled it. In days past, the Knight Wendelin rode there with his squire George. They came on a scene of ruin: fields gone to waste, columns split, statues with broken noses. Vines had once climbed terraces held by the old walls. Now foxes and bats lived among them.

The knight wondered what had befallen the place. He took his horse down to drink. The water tasted sweet, nothing like the salt Dead Sea. Then a sound reached him from a grotto, sad and sweet, like an unhappy woman's voice. Wendelin had ridden out in search of adventures. Seven dragons' tail-tips hung from George's saddle. A woman in peril was the chance a knight could wish for.
the-jungle: Sinclair's 1906 Jungle exposed Chicago meatpacking horrors through Jurgis. It sickened a nation. The Tower library holds the full text. It ground workers. Rats ran. Laws passed. Outrage boiled. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-lani-people:
J. F. Bone writes science fiction about Jac Kennon, a new veterinary graduate with little money and a spaceman ticket. Kennon spots a boxed ad in a medical journal from the planet Kardon. The post offers a five year livestock contract, furnished quarters, a fine hospital, and fifteen thousand credits a year.

Pay that high for a beginner makes him suspect a catch. He checks Kardon currency and finds it sound, then counts what the contract could save toward his own clinic. Bone sets up a frontier job story where a dream offer may hide a hard truth about the Lani.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: The complete memoirs of Jacques Casanova: the whole extraordinary life. Twelve volumes of love, travel, and adventure. The 18th century's most famous autobiography. The whole Casanova in one: twelve volumes, the 18th century entire, the 18th century entire, in one great autobiography.
the-phoenix-and-the-turtle: Shakespeare's mysterious 1601 poem mourning two lovers figured as the phoenix and the turtle-dove, in dense, metaphysical verse. Scholars still argue over which real people the birds stand for, if any. Short, strange, and lovely, it is the most puzzling poem he ever wrote.
the-pilgrim-s-progress-in-words-of-one-s: Bunyan's immortal allegory retold so the youngest children can read it all themselves — in words of one syllable. Christian's flight from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City unfolds in the plainest English. A child's first great classic, made truly his own.
the-poet-at-the-breakfast-table: Oliver Wendell Holmes's Poet at the Breakfast-Table: the Autocrat's successor, wise and witty. Table talk at its most brilliant, full of Boston. The doctor as philosopher. Holmes's talk is as bright as his poetry, boston's Autocrat at his most charming.
the-poetics-of-aristotle: Aristotle's Poetics: the founding work of literary criticism, on tragedy, plot, and catharsis. Terse and profound, it has shaped 2,000 years of thought. The most influential book on literature ever written. Every critic since has argued with Aristotle.
the-professor-at-the-breakfast-table: Oliver Wendell Holmes's Professor at the Breakfast-Table: the Autocrat series continues. Wise, witty, and very Bostonian, it charmed its readers. Table talk raised to art. Holmes's professor is wisdom with a smile, table talk raised to an art.
the-queen-of-the-pirate-isle: Bret Harte's Queen of the Pirate Isle: a children's adventure of pirates. Playful and charming, it shows his lighter side. A delightful juvenile. Child pirates rule Harte's island, a playful juvenile tale, a playful juvenile tale for children.
the-shuttle: Frances Hodgson Burnett's novel about wealthy American heiresses who marry into the British aristocracy. When Bettina Vanderpoel crosses the Atlantic, she finds her younger sister married to a cold, brutal English lord, and sets out to rescue her. A mix of romance, social satire, and sisterly loyalty, it skewers both snobbish lords and the marriage market that traded American money for English titles.
the-story-of-doctor-dolittle: Hugh Lofting's Doctor Dolittle (1920) introduces the vet who talks to animals. Polynesia the wise parrot teaches him. The Tower library holds the full complete text. It tells Dolittle's story wonderfully and kindly. Animals become his grateful patients. Adventures span the wide globe. Children adored the good doctor.
the-story-of-my-life-with-her-letters-18: Helen Keller's Story of My Life, with her letters: the deaf-blind girl's journey into language. Miraculous, moving, and beautifully told, it remains one of the great autobiographies. The triumph of the human spirit. Keller's letters show her mind unfolding in wonder.
the-swiss-family-robinson-told-in-words-: Lucy Aikin retells the beloved castaway adventure using only words of one syllable, so the youngest readers can manage it alone. The shipwrecked family's ingenuity — treehouse, farm, and all — unfolds in the simplest English. A clever, charming first book for children meeting a classic tale.
the-trail-of-the-white-mule: A B. M. Bower Western about the trail of the white mule and the adventures it brings. Cowboy action and the author's authentic range detail fill this lively story. Solid Western entertainment. Bower's Western authenticity never fails her readers.
the-travels-of-sir-john-mandeville: The most popular travel book of the Middle Ages, and one of the great hoaxes of literature. "Sir John Mandeville" claims to have journeyed to China, India, and Prester John's kingdom, describing monsters, marvels, and strange customs, almost all of it invented. Written around 1357, it fed Europe's imagination of the East for two centuries.
the-voyage-of-the-beagle: Charles Darwin's account of the five-year voyage that changed science, from 1831 to 1836. Observing fossils, finches, and earthquakes across South America and the Galápagos, the young naturalist gathered the evidence that would become On the Origin of Species. Lively, curious, and beautifully written, it is the adventure story behind the theory of evolution.
the-voyages-of-doctor-dolittle: Hugh Lofting's 1922 Newbery Medal winner: Doctor Dolittle, who talks to animals, sails to Spider Monkey Island on a series of marvelous voyages. Polynesia the parrot, Chee-Chee, and Jip join the kindest hero in children's books. The high point of the Dolittle series.
the-white-people:
Arthur Machen, a Welsh writer of tales of dread, wrote this strange work in 1904. It here stands in its Wikisource form, from an old print. Machen held that the old pagan world did not die, but hid in the hills and in the blood.

A frame talk on the nature of evil opens the book, in a calm and grave style. Then comes the Green Book, the diary of a girl who roams the Welsh hills to dark rites. The tale is held by many to be one of the high marks of horror in English.
the-winter-s-tale: Shakespeare's late romance of jealousy and redemption: King Leontes destroys his family on a mad suspicion, and only time, and a statue that comes to life, can heal the wound. Spanning sixteen years and two worlds, it moves from tragedy to miracle. One of his most magical plays.
tom-swift-and-his-electric-rifle-or-dari: Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle crackles with high-voltage adventure. The boy inventor tests his amazing new rifle in darkest Africa. Wild beasts and human villains fall before its strange power. Another thrilling exploit for Tom Swift fans everywhere.
un-un-res-seventh-progress-report-of-the:
Mid-1999 in Sierra Leone is the span of the seventh progress report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Observer Mission there, document S/1999/836. Talks at Lomé had just produced a peace deal between the government and the rebel front. The observer mission, UNOMSIL, now had to help turn paper promises into fact.

The report covers the deal's terms, plans for disarming fighters, and the return of people who had fled the war. It also notes deep distrust on all sides. The text captures a hopeful but fragile pause in a brutal war.
vathek-an-arabian-tale: Vathek, an Arabian tale, by William Beckford. Another edition. This book preserves that classic. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
victory-an-island-tale: Joseph Conrad's brooding novel follows Axel Heyst, a loner hiding from the world on a remote Malay island with the young woman he rescued. When three criminals land seeking his supposed treasure, his peace shatters into violence. A story of isolation, love, and moral failure, it ranks among Conrad's most haunting examinations of the human heart.
who-wrote-the-bible-a-book-for-the-peopl: Churchman Washington Gladden brings new Bible learning to plain readers, asking who truly penned the holy books. His fair, godly way helped the faithful take in hard study without loss of faith. A brave, clear landmark of broad-minded church thought.
windsor-castle: Ainsworth set his historical romance at Windsor Castle. The royal fortress looms over the plot. The Tudor tale. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The book preserves that novel. The story holds up. Kept for posterity.
wolfville: Alfred Henry Lewis's Wolfville gathers lively tales of the cowboy town. The Old Cattleman narrates frontier life with rough humor. Gunfighters, gamblers, and cowboys crowd the colorful stories. The old West in all its color and noise.
